results.title: Abel–Ruffini, contrapositive form
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $F$ be a field, let $E$ be a field extension of $F$, and let $n \ge 5$. If $p \in F[X]$ is irreducible and the Galois group of $p$ over $F$ is isomorphic to the symmetric group $S_n$, then no root of $p$ in $E$ is solvable by radicals over $F$.

results.title: Abel–Ruffini for $S_5$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $F$ be a field and let $E$ be a field extension of $F$. If $p \in F[X]$ is irreducible and the Galois group of $p$ over $F$ is isomorphic to the symmetric group $S_5$, then no root of $p$ in $E$ is solvable by radicals over $F$.

results.title: Abel–Ruffini theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ be a natural number. Every complex root of every polynomial with rational coefficients of degree exactly $n$ is expressible by radicals over $\mathbb{Q}$ if and only if $n \le 4$. Here a complex number is expressible by radicals over $\mathbb{Q}$ when it lies in the smallest subfield $S$ of $\mathbb{C}$ such that $z \in S$ whenever $z \in \mathbb{C}$ and $z^k \in S$ for some integer $k \ge 1$.

results.title: Solvable extensions ↔ solvable groups
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $F$ be a field of characteristic zero and let $p \in F[X]$ be a nonzero polynomial. Every root of $p$ in an algebraic closure $\overline{F}$ of $F$ is solvable by radicals over $F$ (obtainable from $F$ by field operations and $n$-th roots inside $\overline{F}$) if and only if the Galois group of $p$ over $F$ is solvable.

results.title: Pascal's rule for binomial coefficients
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all natural numbers $n$ and $i$, $\binom{n+1}{i+1} = \binom{n}{i} + \binom{n}{i+1}$, as an identity of integers.

results.title: Binet's formula for the Lucas numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$, $\varphi^n + \psi^n = L_n$ as real numbers, where $\varphi = (1 + \sqrt{5})/2$ is the golden ratio, $\psi = (1 - \sqrt{5})/2$ is its conjugate, and $L_n$ is the $n$-th Lucas number.

results.title: Greatest common unitary divisor
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $a$ and $b$, $\gcd_1(a, b)$ is the largest natural number that is a unitary divisor of both $a$ and $b$, where a unitary divisor of $n$ is a divisor $d$ of $n \neq 0$ with $\gcd(d, n / d) = 1$. If $a = 0$ or $b = 0$, there is no common unitary divisor and $\gcd_1(a, b) = 0$.

results.title: Symmetry of the greatest common unitary divisor
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all natural numbers $a$ and $b$, the greatest common unitary divisor satisfies $\gcd_1(a, b) = \gcd_1(b, a)$.

results.title: Greatest common unitary divisor with zero on the left
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $b$, the greatest common unitary divisor satisfies $\gcd_1(0, b) = 0$, since $0$ has no unitary divisors.

results.title: Greatest common unitary divisor with zero on the right
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $a$, the greatest common unitary divisor satisfies $\gcd_1(a, 0) = 0$, since $0$ has no unitary divisors.

results.title: Common unitary divisors are at most the greatest one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For natural numbers $a$, $b$ and $d$, if $d$ is a unitary divisor of both $a$ and $b$, then $d \le \gcd_1(a, b)$, where $\gcd_1(a, b)$ is the greatest common unitary divisor of $a$ and $b$.

results.title: The greatest common unitary divisor is a common unitary divisor
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For positive natural numbers $a$ and $b$, the greatest common unitary divisor $\gcd_1(a, b)$ is a unitary divisor of $a$ and a unitary divisor of $b$.

results.title: The greatest common unitary divisor divides its first argument
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For positive natural numbers $a$ and $b$, the greatest common unitary divisor $\gcd_1(a, b)$ divides $a$.

results.title: The greatest common unitary divisor divides its second argument
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For positive natural numbers $a$ and $b$, the greatest common unitary divisor $\gcd_1(a, b)$ divides $b$.

results.title: Positivity of the greatest common unitary divisor
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For positive natural numbers $a$ and $b$, the greatest common unitary divisor $\gcd_1(a, b)$ is positive.

results.title: Biunitary divisors
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $n$, the biunitary divisors of $n$ are the divisors $d$ of $n$ with $\gcd_1(d, n/d) = 1$, where $\gcd_1(a, b)$ denotes the greatest common unitary divisor of $a$ and $b$. For $n = 0$ the set is empty.

results.title: Biunitary divisor sum
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $n$, $\sigma^{**}(n)$ is the sum of the biunitary divisors of $n$, that is, of the divisors $d$ of $n$ with $\gcd_1(d, n / d) = 1$, where $\gcd_1$ denotes the greatest common unitary divisor. Since $0$ has no biunitary divisors, $\sigma^{**}(0) = 0$.

results.title: Characterization of biunitary divisors
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $d$, $d$ is a biunitary divisor of $n$ if and only if $d$ divides $n$, $n \neq 0$ and $\gcd_1(d, n / d) = 1$, where $\gcd_1$ denotes the greatest common unitary divisor.

results.title: Zero has no biunitary divisors
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The set of biunitary divisors of $0$ is empty.

results.title: The biunitary divisor sum of $0$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The sum $\sigma^{**}(0)$ of the biunitary divisors of $0$ equals $0$.

results.title: Biunitary divisors divide
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $d$, if $d$ is a biunitary divisor of $n$, then $d$ divides $n$.

results.title: The biunitary divisor sum of $1$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The sum $\sigma^{**}(1)$ of the biunitary divisors of $1$ equals $1$.

results.title: The biunitary divisor sum of $4$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The sum $\sigma^{**}(4)$ of the biunitary divisors of $4$ equals $5$.

results.title: The biunitary divisor sum of $16$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The sum $\sigma^{**}(16)$ of the biunitary divisors of $16$ equals $1 + 2 + 8 + 16 = 27$.

results.title: The biunitary divisor sum of $27$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The sum $\sigma^{**}(27)$ of the biunitary divisors of $27$ equals $1 + 3 + 9 + 27 = 40$.

results.title: $120$ is biunitary triperfect
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The sum $\sigma^{**}(120)$ of the biunitary divisors of $120$ equals $3 \cdot 120 = 360$.

results.title: Integrating the norm of a derivative within a closed interval
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be a real normed space, let $f : \mathbb{R} \to E$ be any function and let $a \le b$ be real numbers. Then $\int_a^b \lVert f'(t) \rVert \, dt = \int_a^b \lVert f'_{[a,b]}(t) \rVert \, dt$, where $f'(t)$ is the derivative of $f$ at $t$ and $f'_{[a,b]}(t)$ is its derivative at $t$ within $[a, b]$, each taken to be $0$ where it does not exist.

results.title: Length of a $C^1$ curve via its derivative within the interval
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be a real Banach space, let $a \le b$ be real numbers and let $\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to E$ be continuously differentiable on $[a, b]$. Then the total variation of $\gamma$ on $[a, b]$, a priori a value in $[0, \infty]$, equals the real number $\int_a^b \lVert \gamma'_{[a,b]}(t) \rVert \, dt$, where $\gamma'_{[a,b]}(t)$ is the derivative of $\gamma$ at $t$ within $[a, b]$.

results.title: No king permutation of length at least $2$ is separable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $n \ge 2$, every permutation $\sigma$ of $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ in which adjacent entries never differ by exactly $1$, that is, $|\sigma(i + 1) - \sigma(i)| \ne 1$ whenever $i + 1 < n$, contains the classical pattern $2413$ or the classical pattern $3142$. Since the separable permutations are those avoiding both $2413$ and $3142$, no such permutation is separable.

results.title: King permutations
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A permutation $\sigma$ of $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ is a king permutation if adjacent entries never differ by exactly $1$: for every position $i$ with $i + 1 < n$, neither $\sigma(i + 1) = \sigma(i) + 1$ nor $\sigma(i) = \sigma(i + 1) + 1$. Equivalently, $|\sigma(i + 1) - \sigma(i)| > 1$ for all adjacent positions $i$ and $i + 1$.

results.title: Number of ascents of a permutation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ written in one-line notation, $\operatorname{asc}(\sigma)$ is the number of positions $i$ with $i + 1 < n$ and $\sigma(i) < \sigma(i + 1)$.

results.title: Number of descents of a permutation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ written in one-line notation, $\operatorname{des}(\sigma)$ is the number of positions $i$ with $i + 1 < n$ and $\sigma(i + 1) < \sigma(i)$.

results.title: Statistics of the permutation $123$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The identity permutation of $\{0, 1, 2\}$, written $012$ in one-line notation and $123$ after shifting every value up by one, has two ascents, no descents, three left-to-right maxima, one right-to-left maximum, one left-to-right minimum and three right-to-left minima.

results.title: Statistics of the permutation $321$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The reversal permutation $i \mapsto 2 - i$ of $\{0, 1, 2\}$, written $210$ in one-line notation and $321$ after shifting every value up by one, has no ascents, two descents, one left-to-right maximum, three right-to-left maxima, three left-to-right minima and one right-to-left minimum.

results.title: Containing a flat pattern with one bottom label
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a permutation of $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ and let $j \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$. Then $\sigma$ contains the flat partially ordered pattern $P_{j+1}$ of size $4$, in which label $j + 1$ lies below the other three labels (which are mutually incomparable), if there are positions $i_0 < i_1 < i_2 < i_3$ such that $\sigma(i_j) < \sigma(i_m)$ for every $m \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$ with $m \neq j$.

results.title: Even noncrossing partitions and Dyck paths with even descents
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$, there is a bijection between the noncrossing partitions of $\{0, \dots, 2n - 1\}$ all of whose blocks have even size and the Dyck paths of semilength $2n$ all of whose descents have even length. Here the descents of a Dyck path are the lengths of its maximal runs of down steps, one for each peak $UD$: the run of down steps starting at the $D$ of that peak.

results.title: Cross product of plane vectors
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $p = (x_p, y_p)$ and $q = (x_q, y_q)$ in $K^2$, where $K$ is a linearly ordered field, the cross product is $p \times q = x_p y_q - x_q y_p$ (CLRS equation (33.1)).

results.title: Direction of three points
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For points $p_i, p_j, p_k \in K^2$, where $K$ is a linearly ordered field, CLRS's DIRECTION$(p_i, p_j, p_k)$ is the cross product $(p_k - p_i) \times (p_j - p_i)$.

results.title: The ON-SEGMENT test
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For points $p_i = (x_i, y_i)$, $p_j = (x_j, y_j)$ and $p_k = (x_k, y_k)$ in $K^2$, where $K$ is a linearly ordered field, CLRS's ON-SEGMENT$(p_i, p_j, p_k)$ is the Boolean that is true exactly when $p_k$ lies in the bounding box of $p_i$ and $p_j$, that is, $\min(x_i, x_j) \le x_k \le \max(x_i, x_j)$ and $\min(y_i, y_j) \le y_k \le \max(y_i, y_j)$.

results.title: Values of opposite sign
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Two elements $d$ and $e$ of a field with a linear order straddle zero when $d > 0$ and $e < 0$, or $d < 0$ and $e > 0$; that is, $d$ and $e$ are nonzero with opposite signs.

results.title: Collinear-endpoint step of SEGMENTS-INTERSECT
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field, $d \in K$ and $p_i, p_j, p_k \in K^2$. When $d = 0$, this step costs one unit and returns the value of ON-SEGMENT$(p_i, p_j, p_k)$; when $d \neq 0$, it costs nothing and returns false.

results.title: The SEGMENTS-INTERSECT procedure
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $K$ be a field with a linear order and let $p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4 \in K^2$. results.title: Running time of SEGMENTS-INTERSECT
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a field with a linear order and let $p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4 \in K^2$. In the cost model that charges one unit per DIRECTION computation and one per ON-SEGMENT test, SEGMENTS-INTERSECT$(p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4)$ costs at least $4$ and at most $8$.

results.title: SEGMENTS-INTERSECT as a Boolean formula
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a field with a linear order, let $p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4 \in K^2$, and write $d_1 = \mathrm{DIRECTION}(p_3, p_4, p_1)$, $d_2 = \mathrm{DIRECTION}(p_3, p_4, p_2)$, $d_3 = \mathrm{DIRECTION}(p_1, p_2, p_3)$ and $d_4 = \mathrm{DIRECTION}(p_1, p_2, p_4)$. results.title: Points of a segment lie in its bounding box
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field and $p, q, r \in K^2$. If $r$ lies on the closed segment from $p$ to $q$, then ON-SEGMENT$(p, q, r)$ is true, that is, $r$ lies in the bounding box of $p$ and $q$.

results.title: Points of a segment have direction zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field and $p, q, r \in K^2$. If $r$ lies on the closed segment from $p$ to $q$, then the direction $(r - p) \times (q - p)$ is zero, that is, $r$ is collinear with $p$ and $q$.

results.title: A collinear point in the bounding box lies on the segment
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field, write $(u_1, u_2) \times (v_1, v_2) = u_1 v_2 - v_1 u_2$ for the cross product on $K^2$, and let $p, q, r \in K^2$. If $r$ is collinear with $p$ and $q$, that is, the direction $(r - p) \times (q - p)$ is zero, and ON-SEGMENT$(p, q, r)$ is true, that is, $r$ lies in the bounding box of $p$ and $q$, then $r$ lies on the closed segment from $p$ to $q$.

results.title: Values of opposite sign have nonzero difference
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $d$ and $e$ are elements of a linearly ordered field that straddle zero, that is, they are nonzero with opposite signs, then $d - e \ne 0$.

results.title: Zero-crossing parameter of values of opposite sign
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $d$ and $e$ are elements of a linearly ordered field that straddle zero, that is, they are nonzero with opposite signs, then $0 \le d / (d - e) \le 1$.

results.title: A vanishing convex combination of nonzero values forces opposite signs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $d$ and $e$ be nonzero elements of a linearly ordered field. If $a d + b e = 0$ for some $a, b \ge 0$ in the field with $a + b = 1$, then $d$ and $e$ have opposite signs.

results.title: Properly crossing segments meet
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field and $p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4 \in K^2$. Suppose the directions $(p_1 - p_3) \times (p_4 - p_3)$ and $(p_2 - p_3) \times (p_4 - p_3)$ are nonzero with opposite signs, and so are $(p_3 - p_1) \times (p_2 - p_1)$ and $(p_4 - p_1) \times (p_2 - p_1)$. Then the closed segments $p_1 p_2$ and $p_3 p_4$ have a common point.

results.title: Points with direction zero lie on the line
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field and $p, q, r \in K^2$ with $p \neq q$. If $(r - p) \times (q - p) = 0$, then $r = p + \mu (q - p)$ for some $\mu \in K$.

results.title: Collinear case of segment intersection
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field and $p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4 \in K^2$. Suppose the directions $(p_1 - p_3) \times (p_4 - p_3)$ and $(p_2 - p_3) \times (p_4 - p_3)$ are both zero and the closed segments $p_1 p_2$ and $p_3 p_4$ have a common point. Then $p_1$ or $p_2$ lies on the segment $p_3 p_4$, or $p_3$ or $p_4$ lies on the segment $p_1 p_2$.

results.title: Meeting segments cross properly or an endpoint lies on the other
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field and $p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4 \in K^2$, and suppose the closed segments $[p_1, p_2]$ and $[p_3, p_4]$ have a common point. Then either $\mathrm{DIRECTION}(p_3, p_4, p_1)$ and $\mathrm{DIRECTION}(p_3, p_4, p_2)$ are nonzero with opposite signs and $\mathrm{DIRECTION}(p_1, p_2, p_3)$ and $\mathrm{DIRECTION}(p_1, p_2, p_4)$ are nonzero with opposite signs, or $p_1 \in [p_3, p_4]$, or…

results.title: Correctness of SEGMENTS-INTERSECT
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field and let $p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4 \in K^2$. The procedure SEGMENTS-INTERSECT$(p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4)$ returns true if and only if the closed segments $[p_1, p_2]$ and $[p_3, p_4]$ have a common point.

results.title: The floored list maximum is nonnegative
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $L$ of integers, the maximum of $L$ with floor $0$ (which is $0$ for the empty list) is at least $0$.

results.title: Overlap pairs
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The overlap pairs of sequences $x$ and $y$ are the pairs $(x', y')$ in which $x'$ is a suffix of $x$ and $y'$ is a prefix of $y$, or $x'$ is a prefix of $x$ and $y'$ is a suffix of $y$. Prefixes and suffixes include the empty sequence and the whole sequence; the pairs are listed with the suffix–prefix pairs first, and the list can contain repetitions.

results.title: Overlap alignment score
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a substitution score $\sigma$ and a gap score $g$, the overlap score of sequences $s$ and $t$ is the maximum, with floor $0$, of the Needleman–Wunsch scores of the overlap pairs of $s$ and $t$: the pairs $(s', t')$ where $s'$ is a suffix of $s$ and $t'$ a prefix of $t$, or $s'$ is a prefix of $s$ and $t'$ a suffix of $t$.

results.title: Overlap-pair scores are at most the overlap score
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a substitution score and $g$ a gap score. If $(x', y')$ is an overlap pair of sequences $x$ and $y$, then the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x'$ against $y'$ is at most the overlap score of $x$ and $y$, both taken with $\sigma$ and $g$.

results.title: Upper bounds for the overlap score
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Fix a substitution score $\sigma$ and a gap score $g$, and sequences $s$ and $t$. If an integer $b$ is at least the Needleman–Wunsch score of every overlap pair of $s$ and $t$ (a suffix of $s$ with a prefix of $t$, or a prefix of $s$ with a suffix of $t$), then the overlap score of $s$ and $t$ is at most $b$.

results.title: The overlap score is attained
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a substitution score and $g$ a gap score. For all sequences $x$ and $y$ there is an overlap pair $(x', y')$ of $x$ and $y$ such that the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x'$ against $y'$ (with $\sigma$ and $g$) equals the overlap score of $x$ and $y$.

results.title: The overlap score is nonnegative
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every substitution score $\sigma$, gap score $g$ and sequences $s$ and $t$, the overlap score of $s$ and $t$ is at least $0$.

results.title: Infixes
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The infixes of a sequence $y$ are its contiguous substrings: the sequences $l$ such that $y$ is the concatenation of $s$, $l$ and $t$ for some sequences $s$ and $t$, including the empty sequence and $y$ itself. They are listed as the suffixes of the prefixes of $y$, so the list can contain repetitions.

results.title: Fitting score
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a substitution score and $g$ a gap score. The fitting score of a sequence $x$ against a sequence $y$ is the maximum, over all infixes $l$ of $y$ (including the empty one), of the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x$ against $l$ with $\sigma$ and $g$: the best global alignment score of $x$ against a substring of $y$.

results.title: Infix scores are at most the fitting score
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a substitution score and $g$ a gap score. If $l$ is an infix of a sequence $y$, then for every sequence $x$ the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x$ against $l$ is at most the fitting score of $x$ against $y$, both taken with $\sigma$ and $g$.

results.title: Upper bounds on the fitting score
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a substitution score, $g$ a gap score, $x$ and $y$ sequences and $b$ an integer. If the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x$ against every infix of $y$ (with $\sigma$ and $g$) is at most $b$, then the fitting score of $x$ against $y$ is at most $b$.

results.title: The fitting score is attained
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a substitution score and $g$ a gap score. For all sequences $x$ and $y$ there is an infix $l$ of $y$ such that the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x$ against $l$ (with $\sigma$ and $g$) equals the fitting score of $x$ against $y$.

results.title: The overlap score is at most the local score
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a substitution score and $g$ a gap score. For all sequences $x$ and $y$, the overlap score of $x$ and $y$ is at most the local score of $x$ and $y$, both taken with $\sigma$ and $g$.

results.title: The fitting score is at most the local score
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a substitution score and $g$ a gap score. For all sequences $x$ and $y$, the fitting score of $x$ against $y$ is at most the local score of $x$ and $y$, both taken with $\sigma$ and $g$.
